title: Does Fender Own the Stratocaster Design? Inside a Legal Feud Dividing the Global Guitar Business
summary: Fender claims a recent German court ruling provides broad copyright protection over the Strat electric guitar shape. Some competitors disagree.
contentText:
This past May, worldwide musical instrument companies including Yamaha and PRS Guitars received cease-and-desist letters from Munich. The documents, authored by a group of German lawyers, stated that Fender Musical Instruments had newly acquired copyright protection over the iconic Stratocaster electric guitar design. And they demanded that non-Fender-produced Strat-shaped guitars be immediately pulled from the European market.

Fender’s letters had immediate ripple effects across the global musical instrument business. Some companies agreed to work with Fender and change their guitar designs. But others have since retained their own attorneys and fought back, spurring litigation that will test the strength of Fender’s intellectual property right assertions.

“Our client has every right to continue to sell its guitars with Strat-style guitar bodies, whenever and wherever it so chooses, as does the entire [musical instrument] industry on a worldwide basis,” wrote an attorney representing some of Fender’s opponents in a May response. “Efforts by your client to bully competitors based on misrepresentations and overstatements are anti-competitive.”

To fully grasp this brewing legal war requires looking into the past, to a series of prior legal proceedings that stretch back nearly 20 years. It turns out Fender has long been warring with much of the music instrument business over the Strat shape, and the battle has extended from the U.S. trademark tribunal to a German courtroom.

Two Court Cases, Two Decades Apart

Fender first began selling the Stratocaster — a model of double cutaway, S-shaped electric guitars — in the 1950s. The so-called “Strat” was a huge success, and scores of other guitar manufacturers soon began pumping out their own instruments based on the same double cutaway design. It was in 2003 that Fender first tried to stop what it viewed as copycats by filing to federally trademark the Strat shape in the United States.

Seventeen guitar manufacturers and distributors opposed Fender’s application, and the companies were mired in litigation for years. The case was decided against Fender in 2009, when the U.S. Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) rejected the trademark registration.

In that 2009 ruling, TTAB ruled that Fender had forfeited its right to claim trademark protection over the Strat by waiting 50 years to police the alleged infringement. Within that time, the federal tribunal said, the Strat shape had become so ubiquitous in the guitar world that consumers did not view it as connected to Fender — thus rendering the shape “generic” and “non-distinctive,” legal statuses that bar trademark protection in the U.S.

David Gilmour’s Iconic ‘Black Strat’ Smashes All-Time Record For Most Expensive Guitar Ever Sold

TTAB noted, for example, that Paul Simon and Bruce Springsteen both played Sadowsky Strat guitars, and a Tom Anderson Guitarworks’ Strat was featured on The Simpsons . Also, in a 1987 edition of the Random House Dictionary , an image of the Strat shape was featured for the definition of the word “guitar.”

“The evidence overwhelmingly demonstrates that these configurations are so common in the industry that they cannot identify source,” wrote TTAB in the decision.

Things were quiet on the legal front for a long while following TTAB’s ruling. Fender and its competitors both continued to sell guitars in the Strat shape, and neither side went to court over the issue for more than 15 years.

But that changed in 2025, when Fender initiated a new intellectual property lawsuit over the Strat against a Chinese guitar seller named Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments. This time, the forum was very different: Düsseldorf Regional Court in Germany. The legal basis of the case was new, too. Rather than trademark infringement, Fender accused Yiwu of copyright infringement.

Yiwu, which was accused of selling knockoff Fender Strats on the e-commerce site AliExpress, did not respond to the lawsuit. The Düsseldorf court thus entered a default judgment in Fender’s favor this past December. Relying on new German case law around the copyrightability of objects like guitars, that ruling held that the shape designed by Leo Fender is entitled to protection as an “outstanding intellectual creation that reflects his personality.”

“The design as a body without edges gives the ‘Stratocaster’ soft curves that evoke associations with a female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms,” reads the December 2025 ruling. “Such a futuristic, elegant and timeless design of a guitar body, with a fretboard that further accentuates the asymmetrically curved shape, represented something fundamentally new at the time of the ‘Stratocaster’s’ conception and release.”

Demands and Pushback

Fender was quick to celebrate the Düsseldorf court’s ruling, and not just because it won an injunction against Yiwu. The company put out a press release in March announcing that beyond this one case, the decision had established “broad legal protection” for the Strat; Fender said it had acquired an enforceable copyright on the design that could be invoked to bar the manufacture of third-party Strat guitars within the European Union or the importation of such instruments into the continent, even if the sellers are based elsewhere.

Fender followed up on this apparent threat with a series of cease-and-desist letters on May 11, targeting scores of instrument makers that sell their own versions of Strat-shaped electric guitars. Some companies that received the letter are based in Germany, like instrument retailer Thomann, while others are international, like U.S.-based PRS Guitars or the Japanese conglomerate Yamaha.

These letters, an example of which was obtained by Billboard , cited the German default ruling and demanded that the targets “immediately stop manufacturing, selling, marketing or producing such infringing products.”

“We appreciate that copies of our client’s famous ‘Stratocaster’ have been in the market before,” wrote German attorney Richard Dissmann of the international law firm Bird & Bird. “However, with the judgment of the Court of Düsseldorf, it is now clear that our client has a copyright to the shape of the ‘Stratocaster’ guitar body, and that copies of these guitar body constitute copyright infringement.”

After receiving these cease-and-desist letters from Fender, many of the other musical instrument companies lawyered up. A number of them hired Ronald Bienstock , a New Jersey-based attorney with the firm Fox Rothschild. Bienstock specializes in music IP issues, and he previously represented Fender’s opponents in the seminal 2009 trademark case.

Bienstock sent a series of response letters to Dissmann on May 21. These letters, one of which was obtained by Billboard, doubted that Fender has acquired such broad copyright protection. Bienstock argued that Fender cannot enforce this right on anyone other than Yiwu itself, since the Düsseldorf ruling was a default judgment based on an undeveloped record — that is, Yiwu did not respond, provide evidence or go to trial.

How Tariff Chaos Is Throwing the Music Gear Industry Into Turmoil

Bienstock’s letters said that if Fender’s claims were fully litigated in Germany, the country’s courts would reject copyright protection for the Strat.
